title: Guard my tongue (Berakhot 17a)
hook: the closing prayer: my God, guard my tongue from evil

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sim Shalom, the vessel that holds every blessing. Your line was grant peace. Did you make one thing more whole? Today, the very last words before the three steps back. Day five hundred ninety-five.

Here's a test. Think back over yesterday and count the things you said about people who weren't in the room. The coworker's annoying habit. The friend's bad decision. The relative everyone sighs about. Most of us lose count quickly. Now notice where the Amidah puts its last request. You've just spent several minutes standing before God, asking for wisdom, healing and peace. And the first danger the closing prayer worries about as you step back into the day is your own mouth.
screen: `COUNT WHAT YOU SAID ABOUT PEOPLE.` → `MOST OF US LOSE COUNT.` → `THE LAST DANGER: YOUR OWN MOUTH.`

segments.voice: The Talmud, in Berakhot 16b and 17a, records the private prayers different rabbis said after they finished the Amidah. One of them, from Mar the son of Ravina, became the one almost everyone says today. It begins: Elohai, netzor leshoni mera. My God, guard my tongue from evil, and my lips from speaking deceit. It's built on a psalm. In the old Jewish translation: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile." Then it goes on: to those who curse me, let my soul be silent; let my soul be like dust to everyone. Open my heart to Your Torah. Notice the grammar has changed. The whole Amidah speaks as we: heal us, forgive us, bring us back. This prayer suddenly says my. My tongue. My soul. It began as one rabbi's personal prayer, and it still sounds like one. It ends with another psalm: "Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable before Thee, O LORD, my Rock, and my Redeemer." Then the three steps back, a bow to the left, the right and the center, and oseh shalom: may the one who makes peace on high make peace for us. Remember three steps in, and open my lips? The Amidah opened by asking God to open the mouth. It closes by asking God to guard it. Between those two requests, the whole prayer: ancestors, power, holiness, thirteen requests, thanks and peace.
screen: `MAR SON OF RAVINA'S PRAYER.` · `MY GOD, GUARD MY TONGUE.` · `FROM WE TO MY.` · `OPEN MY LIPS, THEN GUARD THEM.` · then, large: `GUARD MY TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: guard your tongue for an hour. Settle, and breathe. Pick the next hour of your day that will have people in it: a meeting, a family dinner, a group chat. Decide now: for that one hour, nothing unkind about someone who isn't there. No eye-rolls, no small digs. Picture the moment the temptation will come, and the quiet you'll put in its place. If you pray, you can say the first line: my God, guard my tongue from evil. The bell holds the time.
Elohai Netzor. My God, guard. The personal prayer after the Amidah, asking to guard the tongue from evil.

Your line: guard my tongue. A week that prayed against harm, for the ones who chose, for Jerusalem, in our own words, with thanks, for peace, and now for a guarded tongue. That's the whole Amidah walked. Today, keep your one guarded hour. Day five hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: After the final blessing of the Amidah, Jews say Elohai netzor quietly, then Psalm 19:15, then take three steps back, bow left, right and center while saying oseh shalom, and stand a moment before stepping forward again.

fork.reveal: My God, guard my tongue from evil, and my lips from speaking deceit: the first thing asked on the way back into the day.

original.note: Hebrew: my God, guard. the opening words of the prayer after the Amidah.

trapdoor: what you thought: a tag-on prayer after the real one.
what it means: the personal guard on the way out: the mouth opened to pray is now asked to stay kind.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 17a, Mar brei d'Ravina; built on Psalm 34:14, closing with Psalm 19:15 and oseh shalom with three steps back (Yoma 53b).
